source.title: Breaking the Token Ceiling: Distilling Smaller, Stronger Byte Models
source.authors: Kalyani Marathe; Artidoro Pagnoni; Tomasz Limisiewicz; Margaret Li; Mike Lewis; Luke Zettlemoyer; Srinivasan Iyer

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. There are minor extraction and table-formatting artifacts, but no apparent cutoff or wrong-document problem.
record.tranche_reason: It measures held-out validation BPB against training FLOPs and fits scaling curves, testing a related scaling-law claim with a fixed-size overtraining sweep rather than the original parameter/data/compute sweeps.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation BPB-versus-FLOPs fits for six training scenarios, downstream error-versus-BPB fits, and explicit comparisons showing that BPB and downstream performance can diverge. It does not test parameter-count scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its comparisons with prior work in Related Work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study fits held-out validation BPB against training FLOPs for fixed-size (~1B) models over a data sweep of about 15B–1.2T units. This is done for six tokenization × objective settings (token and byte vocabularies, cross-entropy and distillation pretraining), three learning rates and two validation sets. It also fits downstream error against BPB and reports how sensitive the fits are. The setting is new (byte-level students, distillation pretraining), with its own results on V1, V5, V6 and V7. It does not reproduce the original parameter or compute-optimal sweeps, so it is T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that validation BPB follows saturating power laws in FLOPs for fixed ~1B models, and that tokenization and training objective change the coefficients and asymptotes. They find token models lead at low compute but plateau, while byte models start worse and improve faster. They conclude BPB does not allow fair comparison across tokenization schemes and objectives. Extrapolated downstream laws predict that End-Of-Token distillation reaches the highest asymptotic averaged accuracy: up to 4% over token distillation, using about one-sixth of the data and about one-fifth of the logit storage. These are extrapolations and are not validated. The authors also note that the choice of validation dataset changes crossover points and asymptotes.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses approximately 1B-parameter models, varies data/compute while comparing token and byte tokenizations and supervised versus distillation objectives, and measures validation BPB; it does not reproduce the original parameter-count or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate, validation dataset, tokenization, and training objective change fitted coefficients or scaling relationships. The paper also reports that alternative residual-weighting schemes are more sensitive for Bytes and Bytes w/ <eot> fits than for Token fits (Appendix D.2).
record.problems: The study holds model size approximately fixed, so it does not establish scaling across parameter counts. Its compute-optimal allocation question is outside scope. Some downstream claims are extrapolations from fitted curves; the paper itself notes validation-dataset sensitivity, and reports that some large runs epoch.
record.rows_left_out: None. The paper's individual benchmark plots and additional per-benchmark results are not separately tabulated as rows here; the included downstream scaling rows use the reported six-benchmark aggregate fits.

untested.parts: Scaling in parameter count; a pure power law where neither model size nor data is the bottleneck (here model size is fixed and the fit saturates to an asymptote c); a span of several orders of magnitude (the data span is about 2 orders).
The paper extrapolates fits to asymptotes and crossover compute (up to 1e25 FLOPs) but never checks the predictions against larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep over model size and token count.
Architecture shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer. Repeated data: some large runs epoch, but this is not analysed separately.
Validation of extrapolated asymptotic accuracies; predictability of individual tasks (only averaged fits are given); fits on machine-translation BLEU against BPB.

missing.what: Downstream accuracy against training FLOPs: all six settings improve with compute; token models plateau; machine-translation BLEU follows an S-shaped curve for byte models (bears on V6 'improves with scale' and on curves bending away from a power law, V7)

Downstream error-vs-BPB fits at LR 1e-3 and 8e-3, which vary widely: e.g. Token Supervised at 1e-3 has γ=3.14 vs 8.78 at 4e-3; Token Distilled at 8e-3 has k=5.6 vs 1292 at 4e-3. Fits on Validation dataset 2 are also omitted
Sensitivity of the asymptote c to leave-one-out fitting and to the residual weighting scheme (byte fits more sensitive; c range up to about 0.038)
Predicted crossover compute and data savings change strongly with the validation dataset (e.g. Marginalize-It 2.04e23 vs 1.60e25 FLOPs; no crossover found at LR 1e-3 on Validation dataset 2)
Measured per-benchmark accuracies at the largest available data scale for each run, against open-weight models

record.verdict_notes: FLOPs are proportional to data here because model size is fixed, so the fitted exponents are data exponents with a model-limited asymptote. They should not be compared directly with Kaplan-style pure power-law exponents. Linking the distilled rows to V5 is a judgement: distillation pretraining is treated as a different training regime. The paper contradicts itself in Section 6.1, point 2, which says byte models 'do not show significantly different scaling behaviors' while the figure captions say they differ significantly. The record's V1 limits_scope label rested on exponents varying with learning rate; that is fit-dependence (V7), not a qualification of V1, so it is replaced here.

versions.untested_parts: Tests BPB versus training FLOPs while model size is approximately fixed and training data varies. It does not separately sweep parameter count or fit loss against token count with compute and parameters controlled.
The paper extrapolates fitted curves, but does not report an independent test showing that fits from small runs predict subsequently observed runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute sweep over parameter count and token count, or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
Depth, width, and other architecture details are not varied at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
The study concerns text pretraining; it does not test other modalities, repeated-data effects as a separate regime, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.

Downstream results are averaged over four multiple-choice and two language-generation benchmarks for the fitted error-versus-BPB laws; the paper does not establish predictability for arbitrary downstream tasks or individual task outcomes.
It examines sensitivity to learning rate, validation dataset, and fitting choices, but does not directly compare Kaplan and Hoffmann compute-optimal allocation estimates.

relationships.condition: Fixed ~1B models (1.28B layer parameters), data swept from about 15B to 1.2T units, six tokenization/objective settings, three learning rates, Validation dataset 1
relationships.reason: Every BPB-vs-FLOPs fit of the form b·x^a + c fits closely, R2 0.997–1.000 (r1–r18). The form is saturating with model size fixed, over about 2 orders of magnitude.
relationships.display_finding: All bits-per-byte versus FLOPs fits achieved R² of 0.997–1.000 with a saturating power-law form over about two orders of magnitude.

relationships.condition: Varying learning rate, validation dataset, tokenization and objective, and (from the text) the fitting choices
relationships.reason: Token Supervised exponent: 0.47 (LR 1e-3), 0.50 (4e-3), 0.52 (8e-3), and 0.37 on Validation dataset 2 (r1, r7, r13, r19). The asymptote c moves from 0.957 to 0.726 between validation sets. Orderings of c flip with learning rate (r5 vs r17). From the text: the residual weighting scheme shifts c by up to about 0.038, and the predicted crossover compute shifts from 2.0e23 to 1.6e25 between validation sets.
relationships.display_finding: Token Supervised exponents were 0.47, 0.50, and 0.52 at learning rates 1e-3, 4e-3, and 8e-3, and 0.37 on the second validation dataset; between validation datasets, asymptote c shifted from 0.957 to 0.726 and predicted crossover compute from 2.0e23 to 1.6e25, learning rate reversed c orderings, and residual weighting shifted c by up to about 0.038.
